Circles On AChord

GeometryCircles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: equal circles sit in a row inside a bigger circle, and a straight line touches the two end circles.
How to play: Drag O up or down to move the row. Use the buttons to change how many circles there are, and tick the boxes for names, the hint or the dotted extras.
3
Look for the math

Drag O as far up or down as you like: the chord PQ changes length, but a short formula always predicts it exactly. The original question was carved on a Japanese tablet in 1871; the answer turns out to be the big radius plus three little ones.

A row of touching circles

Let the big circle have radius R and centre O', and let the middle of the row be O', at distance d from the centre. The N equal circles have radius r, so the row runs from -(N-1)r to (N-1)r. The big circle touches the end circles internally, which puts their centres R-r from the big centre. A right triangle then gives d² + [(N-1)r]² = (R-r)² — the Pythagorean theorem in disguise.

Finding the little radius

Rearranging that equation makes it a quadratic: ((N-1)²-1)r² + 2Rr - (R²-d²) = 0. The applet solves it with the positive root. For N = 3 that is r = (-R + sqrt(9R² - 8d²))/8. Once r is known, every circle in the row is fixed, and the picture can be drawn.

Why the chord has that length

The line PQ is an internal common tangent to the two end circles. If sin φ = 1/(N-1), a short law-of-cosines chase gives PQ = 2 sqrt(R² - (d cos φ)²). The same radical appears when r is eliminated, leaving PQ = 2(R + N(N-2)r)/(N-1). For N = 3 this is PQ = R + 3r, exactly the tablet's answer. The logic test checks all three forms over 505 positions of O for each of the five spinner settings, plus 201 more positions for N = 3: they agree to better than a billionth, so the page's claim holds.

Unger's dotted circles

Tick "Extra" for the dashed circle of radius ρ = Nr, the row of dots on its diameter and two dotted circles centred at O. J. Marshall Unger noticed that those two circles meet the big circle at exactly P and Q. The logic test confirms it: one dotted radius equals OP and the other equals OQ at every position. With ρ the chord formula becomes PQ = 2(R + (N-2)ρ)/(N-1), which for N = 3 is simply PQ = R + ρ. The problem is Problem 1.3.3 from Fukagawa and Pedoe's Japanese Temple Geometry Problems; the applet, its options and this interactive version are Bogomolny's.

Try setting N to 7 and dragging O close to the rim: the row of circles becomes tiny, yet the measured chord still matches the formula.
